The prohibitions apply from 2 February 2025, and the Regulation applies in general from 2 August 2026.

No — both are invalid under the GDPR.

- Recital 32 states that consent must be a clear affirmative act, and silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent, so the pre-ticked box is not valid consent.
- Article 7(3) gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw as to give consent; requiring a posted signed letter fails this, so the letter-only withdrawal term is not acceptable.
- Article 7(3) also confirms withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing before withdrawal, and the data subject must be informed of this right beforehand (also required under Article 13(c)).
- Additionally, Article 7(2) requires consent requests in written declarations to be clearly distinguishable, intelligible and in clear and plain language, and any infringing part of such a declaration is not binding.

Yes — both uses are caught by the prohibition.

- Article 5(1)(f) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, and the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions (Evidence [1], [2]).
- The only exception is where the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons (Evidence [1], [2]).
- The recitals confirm the rationale: given the power imbalance and intrusive nature of such systems in work or education, their placing on the market, putting into service or use to detect emotional state in those situations should be prohibited, with the exception only for systems strictly for medical or safety reasons, such as therapeutic use (Evidence [3], [4]).
- Neither use here is for medical or safety reasons: the lab's putting into service is for scientific research, and the retailer's use is staff mood monitoring in shops — a workplace context.
- Therefore the retailer's use is squarely prohibited, and the lab's putting into service/use is likewise within the prohibition, since no research exemption appears in the cited provisions.
- Note also that even where a system is not prohibited, its use must still comply with other applicable Union and national law on, e.g., personal data protection (Evidence [6]).

The platform must give the user access to its internal complaint-handling system to challenge the removal decision, available for at least six months, starting from the day the user is informed of the decision, free of charge and electronically.

- Article 20(1) requires providers of online platforms to give recipients of the service access to an effective internal complaint-handling system to lodge complaints against decisions on the grounds that information constitutes illegal content, including decisions whether or not to remove or disable access to or restrict visibility of the information.
- Article 20(1) states this access lasts for a period of at least six months following the decision.
- Article 20(2) provides that the six-month period starts on the day the recipient is informed about the decision in accordance with Article 16(5) or Article 17.
- Article 20(1) requires complaints to be lodged electronically and free of charge.
- Article 20(3) adds that the system must be easy to access, user-friendly, and enable sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated complaints.

The company had to notify the Commission without delay and in any event within 2 months after the thresholds were met (Article 3(3)). Failing to comply with that notification obligation can result in a fine of up to 1 % of its total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, where done intentionally or negligently (Article 30).

No — the short-term right to reject is lost.

- Under section 22(1), a consumer loses the short-term right to reject if the time limit passes without it being exercised (unless the trader agrees it may be exercised later).
- Under section 22(3), that time limit is the end of 30 days beginning with the first day after ownership/possession transfer, delivery and (where applicable) installation notification. Ten weeks have passed, so the limit has expired.
- The consumer may instead request or agree to repair or replacement of the goods (section 22(6)); if goods supplied in response do not conform, the time limit for the short-term right to reject is then 7 days after the waiting period ends, or the original limit extended by the waiting period if later (section 22(7)).
- On proof: under section 19(14), goods that do not conform at any time within six months of delivery are taken not to have conformed on the day of delivery, so the consumer need not prove the fault existed at delivery.
- That presumption does not apply if it is established the goods did conform on that day, or if applying it is incompatible with the nature of the goods or how they fail to conform (section 19(15)).

Digital Services Act - 45 million user figure: NOT_FOUND
Digital Markets Act - 45 million user figure: at least 45 million monthly active end users established or located in the Union for a core platform service in the last financial year, identified and calculated per the Annex methodology [1]
Digital Markets Act - additional requirements: at least 10 000 yearly active business users established in the Union in the last financial year, plus meeting those thresholds in each of the last three financial years [1]

The DSA's 45 million figure is not found in the evidence, so the two Acts' figures cannot be compared here. Under the DMA, the 45 million monthly active end users threshold must be accompanied by at least 10 000 yearly active business users and by meeting those thresholds in each of the last three financial years.

AI Act (prohibited AI practice): 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover
Digital Services Act (Commission fine on a very large online platform): 6 % of total worldwide annual turnover
Digital Markets Act (gatekeeper, first offence): 10 % of total worldwide turnover

The maximum fine share is highest under the Digital Markets Act (10 %), followed by the AI Act (7 %) and then the Digital Services Act (6 %).

AI Act (general case) - Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 73(2): not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident
GDPR - Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Art. 33(1): where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of the breach

The GDPR deadline (72 hours) is shorter than the AI Act general deadline (15 days) — 72 hours equals 3 days, so it is 12 days shorter.
